q: Jack leaned over and swept in one of the curly, bobbing snells of the m’sieur’s leader as he answered. “May I help you?” he asked with friendliness of a brother craftsman.
1912 August, Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews, “The Scarlet Ibis”, in Scribner’s Magazine, volume LII, number 2, Charles Scribner’s Sons, page 206, column 2:

Servant. Here, m’sieurs. (The Soldier enters l. The Orderly follows him on.) Soldier. (looking about) We’ll eat here. (To the Servant.) Who live in this house? Servant. Myself, m’sieur—and—myself—and——
1918, Asa Steele, Greater Than War: A War-Time Play in One Act, Philadelphia, Pa.: The Penn Publishing Company, page 7:
Pinot Blanc is, like Mary Poppins, practically perfect in every way. (If you want a bustier and Madonna-like subtlety, I suggest m’sieur would be happier in the California aisle.)
2013 May 27, James Romanow, “Subtle Pinot Blanc a joy”, in Leader-Post, Regina, Sask., page B2:
“Colin—” he started, but Bryan Barker made kissing noises, and Colin’s face grew redder. / “M’sorry,” mumbled Colin, and he walked away.
2016 February 2, Aimée Carter, “Pigeon Pancakes”, in Simon Thorn and the Wolf's Den (Simon Thorn; 1), New York, N.Y.: Bloomsbury Children’s Books, →ISBN, page 16:
“M’sorry, Kassie said. / “It’s all right.” It really was. I was out of that damn house. / “I wanted to—” she started. “I thought we could hang out. It’s Christmas Eve.”
2017 July 25, Glen Erik Hamilton, “Age Twelve, December 24”, in Every Day Above Ground (A Van Shaw Novel; 3), New York, N.Y.: William Morrow, →ISBN, page 247:
M’sorry for being an arsehole patient.
2017 August 14, Ellie Marney, “Amie”, in No Limits, Australia: Bearded Lady Press, →ISBN, page 20:

“He just died. He got ill and died. One day he was here then he wasn’t anymore.” / Adam bit his lip. Charlie’s face had closed up again and Adam decided against probing any more. “M’sorry,” he said uselessly.
2017 September 5, Matthew J. Metzger, chapter 11, in Sharing Secrets, Lincoln, Lincolnshire: Finch Books, →ISBN, page 118:

e: From m (from multisexual) + spec, a clipping of spectrum. Probably modelled on the slightly earlier a-spec (“on the asexual spectrum”).
